Autoencoders learn a representation from which an example can be reconstructed.
Variational autoencoders (VAEs) add a latent-variable probability model and approximate-posterior inference; conditional VAEs also supply context to the generative model.
Let $A$ denote an observed example, $z$ an internal latent vector, and $\hat A$ a reconstructed prediction with the same output shape as $A$.

## Ordinary autoencoders {#autoencoders}

An ordinary autoencoder maps an example to a code and reconstructs the example from that code:

$$
  z=f_\phi(A),
  \qquad \hat A=g_\theta(z).
$$

The encoder parameters $\phi$ and decoder parameters $\theta$ are learned by reducing reconstruction error.
This alone does not specify a probability distribution from which useful new codes can be sampled.

## Variational autoencoders {#vae}

A VAE specifies a prior $p(z)$, a decoder distribution $p_\theta(A\mid z)$, and an approximate posterior $q_\phi(z\mid A)$.
The encoder outputs parameters of a distribution over codes, rather than only one code.
The decoder describes a distribution over possible examples given a code.
These are the recognition and generative models in [Kingma and Welling, §§2.1–2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

An implementation may output a point such as $\hat A=g_\theta(z)$ that parameterises the decoder distribution's mean or location.
The probability model and that point prediction are related objects, but their mathematical types differ.

## Training and generation {#training-and-generation}

Training observes $A$, uses $q_\phi(z\mid A)$ to sample a code, and evaluates how well $p_\theta(A\mid z)$ explains that example.
Generation has no observed answer to encode: it samples $z$ from the prior and then samples an example from the decoder.
An implementation can instead return a decoder mean or location, which is a particular decoding choice.
The [ELBO](../mathematics/elbo.qmd) combines reconstruction likelihood with a KL penalty to train these distributions.

## Objective and differentiable sampling {#objective-and-sampling}

For the unconditional model, write $q_A=q_\phi(z\mid A)$.
The negative ELBO is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  J(A)&=\mathbb E_{q_A}[-\ln p_\theta(A\mid z)]\\
  &\quad+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_A\Vert p(z)).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The first term evaluates reconstruction likelihood, and the second penalises disagreement between the encoder distribution and the prior.
The [ELBO derivation](../mathematics/elbo.qmd) explains the bound and its separate posterior-approximation gap.
For a diagonal Gaussian encoder, one can write a sampled code as

$$
  z=\mu_\phi(A)+\sigma_\phi(A)\odot\epsilon,
  \qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$

Here $\mu_\phi(A)$ and the positive standard-deviation vector $\sigma_\phi(A)$ have the same dimension as $z$, and $\odot$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication.
This separates the random draw from the differentiable encoder outputs.
[Reparameterisation](../mathematics/reparameterization.qmd) gives the full gradient argument and distinguishes variance from standard deviation.

## An action chunk as a conditional example {#objects}

Let $A=(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+H-1})$ be a demonstrated chunk of $H$ actions, and let $o$ be the observation available when that chunk starts.
Each $a_s$ is a vector of robot commands.
The decoder's prediction $\hat A$ has the same action coordinates and shape as $A$.

| Symbol | Role |
|---|---|
| $A$ | Demonstrated actions, available in training data. |
| $\hat A$ | Actions produced by the model. |
| $o$ | Observed context, such as images and joint positions. |
| $z$ | A latent vector used internally to generate a chunk. |

Reconstruction compares $\hat A$ with $A$.
It does not compare the observation with the action, or the latent vector with the action.
The letters do not determine these roles; the model's data flow does.

## Conditional variational autoencoders {#conditioning}

A CVAE supplies $o$ to the generative model:

$$
  z\sim p(z\mid o),
  \qquad A\sim p_\theta(A\mid o,z).
$$

The prior may depend on $o$, but a fixed prior $p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I)$ is also possible.
During training, the approximate posterior can use both the observation and the demonstrated answer, $q_\phi(z\mid A,o)$.
It infers which latent codes help explain this particular demonstrated chunk.

The prior is available before seeing $A$.
The true posterior $p_\theta(z\mid A,o)$ describes latent codes after observing $A$, under the generative model.
The encoder distribution $q_\phi$ approximates that posterior because computing it exactly is generally intractable.
Thus, $q$ is neither the prior nor a distribution over predicted actions.
This extends the posterior distinction in [the VAE paper, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3), and is instantiated for actions in [ACT, §IV-B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.13705#page=5).

## Conditional training and generation {#cvae-training-and-generation}

During training, a dataset provides $(o,A)$.
The encoder uses that pair to construct a latent distribution, a code is sampled, and the decoder predicts $\hat A$ using $(o,z)$.
The target $A$ provides supervision for the reconstruction loss.

During generation, the desired future action chunk is unknown.
The model therefore cannot use an encoder that requires that chunk.
A generic CVAE draws $z$ from its prior and generates using $(o,z)$.
Conditioning on $o$ is what lets the same generative model respond to different scenes.

Original ACT makes a specific deployment choice: it discards the CVAE encoder and fixes $z=0$, the mean of its standard Gaussian prior.
The current images and joint positions still enter the decoder.
Fixing $z$ therefore does not make the policy ignore the scene or repeat the same chunk in every scene.
This is ACT's deterministic decoding choice, not the definition of every CVAE's inference procedure. [ACT, Fig. 4 and Algorithm 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.13705#page=4).

## ACT’s reconstruction objective {#act-objective}

Let $R$ denote reconstruction negative log-likelihood and $K$ the encoder-to-prior KL in the [conditional ELBO](../mathematics/elbo.qmd).
ACT uses an L1 reconstruction term plus a weighted KL term, $J=R+\beta K$.
For fixed-scale independent Laplace decoder coordinates, negative log-likelihood is proportional to an L1 error plus a constant.
This explains the likelihood connection without equating every reconstruction loss with MSE.
Choosing $\beta\ne1$ changes the standard ELBO weighting and should be understood as a modified training objective. [ACT, §§IV-B–IV-C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.13705#page=5).

[MAE](loss.qmd#mae) and [MSE](loss.qmd#mse) compare absolute and squared error; [maximum likelihood](../mathematics/likelihood-and-estimation.qmd#classification) gives the discrete-label likelihood construction.

## Connections {#connections}

[The ELBO](../mathematics/elbo.qmd) derives the reconstruction-plus-KL objective and distinguishes the prior penalty from the posterior approximation gap.
[Reparameterisation](../mathematics/reparameterization.qmd) develops the pathwise gradient and implementation details.
[Gaussian KL](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#gaussian-kl) gives the analytic prior penalty.
The [VAE paper review](../../literature-review/theory/vae.qmd) places the construction in variational inference, and [normalizing flows](../../literature-review/theory/normalizing-flows.qmd) expands the encoder beyond a diagonal Gaussian.
The [ACT review](../../literature-review/action/act.qmd) distinguishes its CVAE encoder from the transformer encoder inside the policy.
